summary: Specifies the syntax of Netnews articles within the Internet Message Format and MIME. It updates the specification to reflect current practice and incorporates incremental changes from other documents. It obsoletes RFC 1036.

plainLanguage.summary: A Usenet article is a piece of text with a set of header fields above it, much like an email. This document defines exactly which header fields an article must have, which are optional, and how each one is written, so that the many servers that exchange articles agree on what they are looking at. The format is a tighter version of the ordinary email format, so anything that reads email can usually read an article too.

what headers are required in a netnews article
what is a message-id in netnews
subtitle: The header fields a Usenet article carries, and the rules that make one article readable by every server.

tldr.problem: Netnews servers flood copies of an article to each other, and each copy is compared with the others by its message identifier, so every article needs a strict, unambiguous format that old and new software can both read.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines the syntax of a Netnews article as a strict subset of the Internet Message Format of RFC 5322, with six mandatory header fields, a set of optional ones, and a restricted syntax for message identifiers that is at most 250 octets long and contains no comments.
tldr.outcome: The document obsoletes RFC 1036, keeps MIME as an integral part of Netnews, and registers the news header fields with IANA. It specifies the article format only; RFC 5537 covers the protocol that carries the articles.

facts.label: Mandatory header fields
facts.value: 6: Date, From, Message-ID, Newsgroups, Path, Subject

today: RFC 5536 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2009. It obsoleted RFC 1036 and was later joined by RFC 5537, which specifies the Netnews protocol itself rather than the article format. The document has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Netnews is a set of protocols for generating, storing and retrieving news articles, whose format is a subset of that used for email messages. It is organised around newsgroups, each a forum with a name and a topic, with the expectation that every reader can see all the articles posted to the groups they take part in.

The protocols most commonly use a flooding algorithm: copies of an article propagate through a network of participating servers. Typically each server keeps only one copy of an article and makes it available on demand to the readers that can reach it.

This document specifies the syntax of Netnews articles in the context of the Internet Message Format of RFC 5322 and the MIME extensions of RFC 2045. It obsoletes RFC 1036, updating the syntax to reflect current practice and to incorporate changes specified in other documents. It is the first of a set of documents that obsolete RFC 1036: this one covers the syntax and semantics of articles, while RFC 5537 covers the protocol issues of articles independently of transport protocols such as the Network News Transfer Protocol in RFC 3977.

The document is deliberately short, because it uses a cite-by-reference method: rather than repeating the contents of other standards, it points at them and adds only the restrictions that Netnews needs. Appendix B lists the changes from RFC 1036, among them multiple addresses in the From field, MIME as an integral part of Netnews, new optional fields such as Archive, Injection-Info and User-Agent, the deprecation of the Lines field, and the removal of the convention that treated a subject starting with cmsg as a control message.
sections.plainLanguage: Netnews is the system behind Usenet. Articles are copied from server to server, and each server keeps one copy and hands it out to readers on request. This document defines the text format of an article. It is the first of two documents replacing the 1987 specification: this one covers the format, and another covers the protocol that moves articles around.

sections.title: The Vocabulary of Netnews
sections.content:
The document defines the terms the rest of the specification depends on.

  • An article is the unit of Netnews, the counterpart of a message in email. A proto-article is one that has not yet been injected into the news system and may still lack some mandatory header fields.
  • A message identifier is a unique identifier for an article, usually supplied by the user agent that posted it or, failing that, by the news server. It distinguishes the article from every other article ever posted anywhere, and articles with the same identifier are treated as the same article whatever differences their bodies or header fields hold.
  • A newsgroup is a forum with a name for articles on a specific topic. An article is posted to one group or several, and posting to several is called crossposting, which differs from posting the same text as separate articles.
  • A group may be moderated, in which case submissions are not posted directly but mailed to a moderator for consideration and possible posting. The moderator is typically a person but may be implemented partly or entirely in software.
  • A poster composes and submits a potentially compliant article to a user agent; a reader is the person or software that reads articles. A followup is an article that responds to an earlier article, its precursor, and every followup carries a References header field naming that precursor.
  • A control message is an article marked as carrying control information, and a news server receiving one may take actions beyond filing and passing it on, subject to the policies of that site.
  • A news server accepts articles from a user agent, makes articles available to user agents, and exchanges articles with other news servers. A user agent helps posters submit proto-articles, fetches articles and presents them to a reader, and helps the reader write articles and followups. The generic term agent covers both.

An agent is said to generate a construct if it did not exist before the agent created it, for example a message made from text supplied by a user, or an Injection-Info header field created by a server for a newly posted message. An agent is said to accept a construct if another entity generated it and passed it over, and the agent processed it without treating it as a format or protocol error.
sections.plainLanguage: The document separates what a reader sees from what the servers need to know. An article before it reaches the network is a proto-article and may still be missing fields. A message identifier is what makes an article unique, so servers can recognise a copy they already have. A control message is an article that tells servers to do something rather than just file it.

sections.title: The Article Format
sections.content:
An article is conformant to this specification if it conforms to the format of RFC 5322 and to the additional requirements of this document. An article that uses the obsolete syntax of Section 4 of RFC 5322 is NOT conformant, with two exceptions: articles are conformant if they use the obs-phrase construct, a phrase such as a name without quotes, but agents MUST NOT generate such syntax; and articles are conformant if they use GMT as the time zone. Agents conforming to this specification MUST generate only conformant articles.

The grammar in this document restricts the syntax of RFC 5322 and is intended to be more restrictive, so an article must satisfy both the ABNF of RFC 5322 and the restrictions given here, whether those restrictions are written as text or as ABNF. The header fields are written in Augmented Backus-Naur Form, as in RFC 5234, reusing constructs from RFC 5322, RFC 2045 as updated by RFC 2231, and RFC 3986. The message identifier is defined more strictly than in Section 3.6.4 of RFC 5322.

Four general rules apply to every header field. Agents MUST generate header fields so that at least one space follows the colon separating the name from the body, for compatibility with deployed software including NNTP servers, and MAY accept fields that lack the space. Every line of a header field body, including the first and any folded lines, MUST contain at least one non-whitespace character, so no header field body can be empty; that is why the document uses a stricter definition of unstructured than RFC 5322 does. Compliant software MUST NOT generate header field lines of more than 998 octets, though it MAY accept them, and there is no limit on the number of lines a field may be folded into. The character set for header fields is US-ASCII, and any non-ASCII character MUST be encoded with the MIME mechanisms of RFC 2047 and RFC 2231.

User agents MUST meet the definition of MIME conformance in RFC 2049 and MUST also support RFC 2231. That level of conformance covers internationalisation and multimedia in message bodies and in header fields. For the purposes of Section 5 of RFC 2047, all the header fields defined in Section 3 of this standard count as extension message header fields, so encoded words may be used in any unstructured field or in any comment or phrase inside a structured field. User agents MAY accept and generate other MIME extension header fields, and SHOULD in particular accept Content-Disposition and Content-Language.
sections.plainLanguage: An article is an email message with extra rules, and the rules are mostly about being strict. A space must follow the colon in every header field, no field may be empty, a single line of a field may not be longer than 998 characters, and anything outside US-ASCII has to be encoded the MIME way. Two old-fashioned things are still allowed: a name written without quotes in the From field, and the GMT time zone.

sections.title: News Header Fields
sections.content:
The news header fields extend those defined in Section 3.6 of RFC 5322. Each of them MUST NOT occur more than once in an article. The fields Control, Distribution, Followup-To, Lines, Newsgroups, Path, Supersedes and Xref, and the Message-ID field from RFC 5322, do not allow comments, because news servers often have to process these fields very quickly.

Every conformant article MUST have exactly one of each of six fields: Date, From, Message-ID, Newsgroups, Path and Subject. The Date field is the one of RFC 5322, except that agents MUST accept date-time constructs using the GMT zone because that practice is widespread. The From field carries a mailbox list. The Newsgroups field names the groups the article is posted to, written as dot-separated components of letters, digits and the characters plus, minus and underscore; a component SHOULD NOT consist solely of digits and SHOULD NOT contain uppercase letters, and components starting with an underscore are reserved for future versions of the standard. Components starting with plus or minus are reserved for private use. Groups whose first component is example, the group poster, and several other names are reserved and MUST NOT be used for ordinary newsgroups.

The optional fields add the rest of the news vocabulary. Approved names the people or entities approving the article, which matters for moderated articles and group control messages. Archive states whether the poster permits redistribution from public long-term archives, with a body of no or yes. Control marks the article as a control message and gives the action to take. Distribution limits where the article may be distributed, and Expires gives a date after which it should be removed. Followup-To names where a reply to the article should be sent. Injection-Date records when the article entered the network, and Injection-Info records the injecting server, with parameters for the posting host, the posting account, logging data and where complaints about the poster should be sent. Organization gives a short phrase for the poster's organisation. References names the precursor of a followup, Summary holds a one-line summary, Supersedes names an article that this one replaces, and Xref names the other groups the article was crossposted to. The Lines field is obsolete.
sections.plainLanguage: Six header fields must appear exactly once in every article: the date, the sender, the message identifier, the groups, the path and the subject. Everything else is optional. Among the optional ones, Injection-Info records where the article entered the network and where to complain about it, and Control tells a server to do something other than just file the article.

sections.title: Message Identifiers
sections.content:
The Message-ID header field holds a unique message identifier. Netnews depends on identifier uniqueness and fast comparison more than email does, and some news software and standards might have trouble with the full range of message identifiers RFC 5322 allows, so this document restricts the syntax.

The identifier is written as the left part, an at sign and the right part, wrapped in angle brackets, and the whole thing MUST NOT be more than 250 octets long. The length limit exists so that systems that accept message identifiers as a parameter when referencing an article, such as NNTP, can rely on a bounded length. The left part is a dot-atom-text and the right part is either a dot-atom-text or a literal in square brackets that contains none of the characters greater-than, left or right square bracket or backslash.

Four differences from RFC 5322 matter. Comments are not allowed inside the Message-ID field. Neither a greater-than sign nor whitespace can occur inside the identifier, so a simple comparison of octets always settles whether two identifiers are the same. The right part is case-sensitive, even though it is usually derived from a domain name, so it must not be altered during later transmission or copying, and an implementation MUST NOT generate a Message-ID whose only difference from another is the case of characters in the right part. And when generating an identifier, implementations SHOULD use a domain name as the right part, because domain literals are troublesome, as many IP addresses are not globally unique, while domain names are more likely to produce unique identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: The message identifier is the part of an article that says which article it is. It is short, at most 250 characters, and it contains nothing that could be read two ways, so a server can compare two identifiers byte for byte and be sure of the answer. The part after the at sign is treated as case-sensitive and must not be changed once the article is on its way.

sections.title: The Path Header Field
sections.content:
The Path field records the route an article has taken since it was injected into the Netnews system. Every agent that processes an article must prepend at least one path identity to the field body. The main reason is so that news servers avoid sending an article to sites already known to have it, in particular the site it came from; it also allows statistics to be gathered and the route of an article to be traced.

A path identity is a name identifying a site. It takes the form of a domain name with two or more dot-separated components, or a single name with no dots. The identities in the path list, read from right to left, give the successive agents through which the article has passed. A double exclamation mark means that the agent to its left verified the identity of the agent to its right before accepting the article, whereas a single exclamation mark implies no such claim. The last entry, the tail entry, may be the string not-for-mail, which is often used because the path was once used as a mail address for the sender.

The Path field may also carry a path diagnostic, an item inserted for purposes other than naming a site; the keywords used for this are described in RFC 5537. One use of a diagnostic is to record an IP address, and IPv6 addresses are allowed, which permits the colon character; the document notes that this may cause interoperability problems at older sites that treat a colon as a delimiter and have neighbours whose names are four or fewer characters of hexadecimal digits. The use of IPv4 addresses in the field is deprecated, though still acceptable in the deprecated diagnostic form.
sections.plainLanguage: The Path field is the trail an article leaves as it moves from server to server. Each server that handles the article adds its own name at the front, so the field reads as the list of servers, most recent first. That lets a server avoid sending an article back where it came from, and lets an operator trace the route an article took.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Netnews article format provides no security services of its own: no confidentiality, no authentication of the sender and no non-repudiation. Those have to be layered above the format, with protocols such as S/MIME in RFC 3851 or PGP/MIME in RFC 3156, or below it, with secure versions of the news transport protocols.

The document singles out one risk that the format itself creates. Message identifiers must be unique, and an article may be refused in server-to-server transfer if the identifier has already been seen. If a malicious agent can predict the identifier of an article, it can post its own article with the same identifier, possibly to a quite different group, and stop the real article from propagating. Agents that generate message identifiers SHOULD therefore ensure that they are unpredictable.

On MIME, the document points out that the range of encodings allowed for parameters permits constructs that simple parsers may fail to parse correctly, and gives two examples of hard-to-parse Content-Type headers. Such parsing deficiencies may be used as part of an attack. Further security considerations are discussed in RFC 5537.
sections.plainLanguage: The article format itself offers no protection: anyone can write an article that claims to be from anyone else. Sending a service such as S/MIME is what adds confidentiality and a signature. The document also warns that if the message identifier can be guessed, an attacker can post a false article under the same identifier and stop the real one from being delivered, so the identifier should be hard to predict.

sections.title: Registered Header Fields
sections.content:
IANA has registered the header fields of this document in the Permanent Message Header Field Repository, following the procedures of RFC 3864. Each registration records the field name, the protocol it applies to, its status, the change controller and the documents that specify it.

The fields registered as standard by this document are Approved, Archive, Comments, Control, Date, Distribution, Expires, Followup-To, From, Injection-Date, Injection-Info, Keywords, Message-ID, Newsgroups, Organization, Path, References, Reply-To, Sender, Subject, Summary, Supersedes, User-Agent and Xref. The Lines field is registered as deprecated, and fields carried over from the earlier Netnews specifications, such as Also-Control, Article-Names, Article-Updates, Date-Received, NNTP-Posting-Date, NNTP-Posting-Host, Posting-Version, Relay-Version and See-Also, are registered with the status obsoleted and point at the document that replaced them.
sections.plainLanguage: Every field this document defines has been registered with IANA, which keeps a list of the header fields that exist and which document each one belongs to. Fields that earlier Netnews specifications defined are marked as obsolete on that list, along with the document that replaced them.

items.title: Date
items.text: When the article was written, as a date-time with a numeric zone.

items.title: From
items.text: The mailbox of the poster, or a list of mailboxes.

items.title: Message-ID
items.text: The identifier that makes the article unique, at most 250 octets.

items.title: Newsgroups
items.text: The groups the article is posted to, as dot-separated names.

items.title: Path
items.text: The trail of servers the article has passed through.

items.title: Subject
items.text: A short description of the article.

viz.caption: OPTIONAL HEADER FIELDS AND WHAT THEY DO

items.title: Approved
items.text: The people or entities who approved the article, used for moderated groups.

items.title: Archive
items.text: Whether the poster permits redistribution from public archives.

items.title: Control
items.text: Marks the article as a control message and gives the action to take.

items.title: Distribution
items.text: Limits the areas in which the article may be distributed.

items.title: Expires
items.text: The date after which the article should be removed.

items.title: Followup-To
items.text: Where a reply to the article should be sent.

items.title: Injection-Info
items.text: How the article entered the network, and where to complain about it.

items.title: Supersedes
items.text: The article that this one replaces.

data.title: fields
data.code:
fields          =/ *( approved /
                     archive /
                     control /
                     distribution /
                     expires /
                     followup-to /
                     injection-date /
                     injection-info /
                     lines /
                     newsgroups /
                     organization /
                     path /
                     summary /
                     supersedes /
                     user-agent /
                     xref )

data.title: msg-id
data.code:
message-id      =  "Message-ID:" SP *WSP msg-id *WSP CRLF

msg-id          =  "<" msg-id-core ">"
                   ; maximum length is 250 octets

msg-id-core     =  id-left "@" id-right

id-left         =  dot-atom-text

id-right        =  dot-atom-text / no-fold-literal

no-fold-literal =  "[" *mdtext "]"
